procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 29.05.2009 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1419, 1430, 1518, 898 of 2004 and Government Appeal No. 5270 of 2005.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court reversed the judgment of conviction passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Kanpur in Sessions Trial No. 164/2002 dated 22.01.2004 under Sections 302 read with 149, 307 read with 149, 148 IPC and Section 7 of Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1932. The High Court in Government Appeal no. 5270 of 2005 preferred by the appellant-State, dismissed the appeal against the acquittal of accused no.1-respondent (Wasif Haider) for offences under Sections 25 and 27 of Arms Act, 1959 and Sections 4 and 15 of Explosive Substances Act, 1908, while affirming the judgment dated 3.8.2005 passed by the Additional Sessions judge, Kanpur acquitting the accused no.1-respondent (Wasif Haider) in Sessions Trial No. 143 and 144 of 2002.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals by special leave were filed against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

directions: Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Appeal against the acquittal of the accused.

facts: The trial court had initially convicted the accused persons.
On appeal, the High Court acquitted all the accused.
The State of Uttar Pradesh then filed these appeals before the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's judgment of acquittal.
law: In an appeal against acquittal, an appellate court should only interfere if there is perversity of fact and law.
The presumption of innocence is further reinforced for an accused person who has been acquitted by a court.
The Supreme Court requires compelling reasons to entertain an appeal challenging an order of acquittal.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's judgment and found no perversity in it.
The Court concurred with the High Court's decision, noting that the case was ridden with "multiple investigative laches and flaws which goes to the root of the matter."
The Court determined that there were no compelling reasons to interfere with the High Court's order of acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: Finding no perversity in the High Court's judgment and no compelling reasons to interfere, the Supreme Court dismissed the state's appeals and upheld the acquittal of the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Appeal against the acquittal of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The identification of the accused-respondents was properly conducted with due precautions and procedure.
Prosecution witnesses clearly identified the accused persons in the identification parade and in court.
There was no inordinate delay in conducting the Test Identification Parade (TIP).
The High Court erred by not placing reliance on the TIP, as there was nothing on record to vitiate its results.
There was sufficient evidence to prove the culpability of the accused-respondents, and the Sessions Judge had correctly convicted them.
respondent_arguments: Accused-respondent no. 2 was implicated solely based on an uncorroborated confessional statement of a co-accused.
There is no other incriminating evidence available on record against accused-respondent no. 2.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In the absence of compelling reasons, the court will not entertain an appeal challenging an order of acquittal, particularly where there is no perversity in the lower court's judgment.
obiter: The prosecution must establish its case against the accused by leading evidence that is accepted by the standards known to criminal jurisprudence, regardless of the circumstances of the crime.
There can only be one set of rules and standards for trials and judgments in criminal cases unless a statute provides for a special exception.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concurs with the High Court's acquittal because the case is ridden with multiple investigative laches and flaws that go to the root of the matter. Despite the gravity of the offense, the lapses in the investigation disabled the prosecution from proving the culpability of the accused, and the benefit of the doubt arising from such an inefficient investigation must be bestowed upon the accused.
legal_tests_applied: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court would interfere only where there exists perversity of fact and law.
The presumption of innocence is further reinforced against the acquitted-accused by having a judgment in his favor.

A suspicion, however grave it may be cannot take place of proof, i.e., there is a long distance between “may be” and “must be”, which must be traversed by the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution failed to link the chain of circumstances so as to dispel the cloud of doubt about the culpability of the accused-respondents.
The case is ridden with multiple investigative laches and flaws which goes to the root of the matter.
The prosecution has also failed to adduce any independent witness.
The evidences adduced by the prosecution witnesses do not inspire the confidence of this Court.
The prosecution has absolutely failed to substantiate the charges by means of evidence, particularly for the charge under Section 307 of IPC.
There exists no perversity in the judgment of the High Court.
why_respondent_won: The presumption of innocence was further reinforced by the High Court's judgment of acquittal.
The benefit of doubt arising out of an inefficient investigation must be bestowed upon the accused.
The prosecution's case was based on suspicion, which cannot take the place of proof required to establish a case beyond a reasonable doubt.
policy_considerations: The accused cannot be expected to relinquish his innocence at the hands of an inefficacious prosecution, which is ridden with investigative deficiencies.

Although we acknowledge the gravity of the offence alleged against the accused-respondents and the unfortunate fact of a senior official losing his life in furtherance of his duty we cannot overlook the fact that the lapses in the investigation have disabled the prosecution to prove the culpability of the accused.
